summary.text: The immune system is a network of biological systems that protects an organism from diseases.
It detects pathogens such as viruses, bacteria, and parasites, along with cancer cells and foreign objects, and tells them apart from the organism's own healthy tissue.
Its defenses are layered: physical barriers first, then the innate response, then in vertebrates the adaptive system, which keeps a memory of pathogens it has met.

items.prompt: A bacterium slips past the skin and the body reacts at once, but with a general response not aimed at that exact germ. Which defense is this?

options.label: The innate immune system
The adaptive immune system
The physical barriers
Immunodeficiency

items.explain: If a pathogen breaches the barriers, the innate immune system provides an immediate but non-specific response.

items.prompt: Someone recovers from a virus. Months later the same virus returns and the body hits it faster and harder. What explains this?

options.label: The skin barrier grew thicker after the first infection
The virus weakened itself over time
The adaptive system kept its improved response as a memory
The body forgot the virus and started fresh

items.explain: The improved response is retained after the pathogen is gone as immunological memory, which allows faster and stronger attacks on later encounters.

items.prompt: A person's hyperactive immune system attacks their own thyroid as if it were a foreign invader. What is this called?

options.label: Immunodeficiency
Vaccination
Phagocytosis
Autoimmunity

items.explain: Autoimmunity results from a hyperactive immune system attacking normal tissues as if they were foreign organisms; Hashimoto's thyroiditis is one example.

items.prompt: A patient with HIV/AIDS has repeated, life-threatening infections. What is going on in their immune system?

options.label: It is less active than normal
It is hyperactive and attacking healthy tissue
It is working normally but has met too many pathogens
It is unable to produce any kind of barrier

items.explain: Immunodeficiency occurs when the immune system is less active than normal, which can result from conditions such as HIV/AIDS.

items.prompt: Why does a healthy immune system not normally attack the body's own tissue?

options.label: It only attacks things that are moving
It can tell the body's own molecules from foreign ones
It only attacks after a vaccination
It cannot reach tissue inside the body

items.explain: Both innate and adaptive immunity depend on distinguishing self from non-self molecules.

options.label: A cell that produces white blood cells in bone marrow
A barrier of skin and mucus that blocks germs
A substance that binds specific immune receptors and triggers a response
A medicine that suppresses the immune system

items.explain: Antigens are defined as substances that bind to specific immune receptors and elicit an immune response.

paragraphs.heading: A body's defense network
paragraphs.text: The immune system is a set of linked biological systems that protects an organism from disease. It detects a wide range of pathogens, such as viruses, bacteria and parasites, along with cancer cells and foreign objects like wood splinters, and it tells all of these apart from the body's own healthy tissue. Nearly every organism has some kind of immune system. Even bacteria have a simple one, made of enzymes that guard against viral infection.

paragraphs.heading: Layers of defense
paragraphs.text: The defenses are layered, and each layer is more specific than the one before. Physical barriers come first and keep pathogens like bacteria and viruses from getting in. If a pathogen breaks through, the innate immune system responds right away, but not in a targeted way. If pathogens slip past that as well, vertebrates have a second layer, the adaptive immune system, which the innate response switches on.

paragraphs.heading: Walls, washes and chemicals
paragraphs.text: Barriers can be mechanical, chemical or biological. Skin, insect exoskeletons, the waxy cuticle of most leaves and the shells of eggs laid outside the body are mechanical barriers. Because a body cannot be sealed off completely, openings such as the lungs and intestines get extra protection: coughs and sneezes throw out pathogens, tears and urine flush them away, and mucus traps microorganisms. Chemical defenses include antimicrobial peptides like the β-defensins, lysozyme in saliva and tears, and gastric acid in the stomach. In the gut and genitourinary tract, commensal flora act as a biological barrier, competing with harmful bacteria for food and space.

paragraphs.heading: Innate and adaptive
paragraphs.text: Many species have two main immune subsystems. The innate system gives a preset response to broad groups of threats, usually triggered when pattern recognition receptors spot features shared across large groups of microbes, or when damaged or stressed cells send alarm signals. The adaptive system instead tailors its response to each threat by learning to recognize molecules it has met before. Both depend on telling self molecules, the body's own parts, from non-self molecules, which are foreign. Antigens are one class of non-self molecules: substances that bind to specific immune receptors and provoke an immune response.

paragraphs.heading: Memory and vaccines
paragraphs.text: Jawed vertebrates, including humans, have a more sophisticated defense. During an infection, adaptive immunity sharpens its recognition of the pathogen, a process called somatic hypermutation. That improvement is kept after the pathogen is gone, as immunological memory, so the next encounter with the same pathogen meets a faster and stronger attack. This memory is the basis of vaccination.

paragraphs.heading: When it goes wrong
paragraphs.text: When the immune system malfunctions, the result can be cancer, inflammatory diseases or autoimmune diseases. In immunodeficiency the system is less active than normal, which leads to recurring and life-threatening infections. In humans this can come from a genetic disease such as severe combined immunodeficiency, from acquired conditions such as HIV/AIDS, or from immunosuppressive medication. In autoimmunity an overactive system attacks normal tissue as if it were foreign. Common examples are rheumatoid arthritis, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, systemic lupus erythematosus and diabetes mellitus type 1.
